narrative:
The model predicts you have a 17% chance of failing your final year, which is why the school requires you to take remedial courses as a precaution. Although this probability is not extremely high, the system flags it as enough of a risk to warrant extra support.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your number of past class failures, your desire to pursue higher education, and your mother's level of education. Surprisingly, having no previous failures was the strongest element pulling the prediction toward passing. Your clear ambition to continue studying beyond high school also worked in your favor, pushing the outcome away from failure. However, your mother's secondary education level worked against you, pulling the prediction toward failing. Among students who passed, a much higher proportion had mothers with higher education, so this background appears to make success statistically harder according to the model.

To improve, focus on maintaining the positive momentum from having no past failures and your strong ambition. Consider reaching out for extra academic help early, especially in subjects where you feel less confident, and try to reduce your 14 absences—well above the average of fewer than 4 days among students who passed. Building consistent study habits now can turn that 17% risk into a much safer outcome.
